evals.prompt: Compare mixed-precision training on `ml.g5` / `ml.g6e` / `ml.p5` (Ampere/Hopper GPUs) versus older `ml.g4dn` (T4 Turing GPUs): why did FP16 without `GradScaler` produce `NaN` losses, when should we use `torch.bfloat16`, and how does `gradient_accumulation_steps` achieve an effective batch size of `128` when only `micro_batch_size = 4` fits per GPU across `4` GPUs?
evals.expected_output: Explains that Ampere/Hopper (`ml.g5`, `ml.g6`, `ml.g6e`, `ml.p4d`, `ml.p5`) natively support **`torch.bfloat16`** (`torch.amp.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)` — same dynamic exponent range as FP32, eliminating overflow `NaN`s without `GradScaler`), whereas T4 (`ml.g4dn`) requires FP16 + **`torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler`** (with FP32 master weights). Computes `gradient_accumulation_steps = 128 / (4 GPUs * 4 micro_batch) = 8` steps before `optimizer.step()`.
expectations: Activates the sagemaker-training-architect skill
Contrasts `torch.bfloat16` on Ampere/Hopper (`ml.g5`/`ml.g6e`/`ml.p4d`/`ml.p5`, FP32 dynamic range without `GradScaler`) against FP16 + `GradScaler` on Turing (`ml.g4dn`)
Calculates `gradient_accumulation_steps = 128 / (4 × 4) = 8`
